newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela Central Bank may tweak monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela Central Bank may tweak monetary policy.

text.p: Venezuela's Central Bank may tweak its monetary policy in light of higher government spending forecast for the year, but will hang tight with its current foreign exchange policy, a Central Bank director said.

Exchange rate policy will continue to "promote a fall in inflation while also allowing a reasonable degree of flexibility that avoids market distortions and negative effects," Bank director Carlos Hernandez Delfino told Reuters.
Venezuelan inflation has steadily fallen since prices and exchange rate controls were liberalized last April -- but at the expense of an increasingly overvalued bolivar.
Although the bolivar floats freely between gently depreciating bands, its has only slipped some three percent against the dollar in the past year -- even as inflation has topped 70 percent.

Reducing inflation further -- March's 1.6 monthly rate was the lowest in five year -- remains a high government priority. Yet official inflation targets for the year have been upped to 35 percent, largely after a 70 percent public sector wage increase was agreed in February.
Hernandez said monetary policy would be determined by the state of Venezuelan fiscal accounts -- seen deteriorating from last year's one percent central government surplus due to the wage hike.
"Changes in these (fiscal) accounts will lead to some adjustments in the Bank's approach to monetary policy," Hernandez said. He details, except that the changes "are still being studied."

"Reducing inflation requires a high degree of financial, fiscal and monetary discipline, which also requires a high degree of institutional coordination between the Finance Ministry, PdVSA and the Bank," he added.
PdVSA is Venezuela's state-owned oil industry.

Other than intervention in the exchange markets, Central Bank monetary tools are currently limited to open market operations with Bank-backed paper, called TEMs, in weekly auctions. Primarily used to soak-up excess liquidity, the TEMs are also taken as benchmark for wider interest rates.
